title: Mean vs. median under skew
body: If a distribution is relatively symmetric the mean and median are close, if it is skewed right the mean is usually larger than the median, and if it is skewed left the mean is usually smaller than the median.
ced_evidence: 1.8.B.1: If a distribution is skewed right, then the value of the mean is usually larger than the median.

title: Boxplot
body: A boxplot is a graph of the five-number summary, with a box spanning Q1 to Q3, a line at the median, whiskers to the extreme non-outlier values, and outliers marked separately.

items.label: Box
items.meaning: Represents the middle 50% of the data, with ends at Q1 and Q3

items.label: Median line
items.meaning: Line inside the box at the median

items.label: Whiskers
items.meaning: Lines representing 25% of the data each, extending from Q1 to the minimum and from Q3 to the maximum

items.label: Whisker ends when outliers exist
items.meaning: The whiskers extend to the most extreme data values that are not outliers

items.label: Outliers
items.meaning: Usually denoted with an asterisk or other symbol

ced_evidence: 1.8.A.2: A boxplot is a graphical representation of the five-number summary (minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, maximum).

title: Census
body: A census consists of recording information from all items or individuals in a population.
ced_evidence: 1.10.B.1: A census consists of recording information from all items or individuals in a population.

title: Three components of an investigative question
body: An investigative question has three components: one guiding data collection, one guiding the analysis choice, and one indicating the type of conclusion.

items.label: First component
items.meaning: Guides data collection and is phrased in terms of the variable(s) of interest

items.label: Second component
items.meaning: Guides the data analysis choice: for a hypothesis test, make clear the parameter and the direction of the alternative; for a confidence interval, make clear the parameter and the goal of estimating it within a range of values

items.label: Third component
items.meaning: Indicates the type(s) of conclusion applicable: the population to which conclusions apply and, for an experiment with random assignment, a cause-and-effect conclusion

title: Experiment
body: An experiment is a study in which a researcher assigns conditions, or treatments, to experimental units to explore an investigative question of interest about the population.
ced_evidence: 1.10.C.1: An experiment is a study in which a researcher assigns conditions, or treatments, to experimental units

title: Confounding variable (observational study)
body: A confounding variable in an observational study provides an alternative explanation for the observed relationship between the explanatory and response variables and must be associated with both of them.
ced_evidence: 1.10.D.5: To be a confounding variable, a variable must be associated with both the explanatory variable and the response variable.

title: Simple random sample (SRS)
body: In a simple random sample of size n, every sample of size n has the same chance of being selected.
ced_evidence: 1.11.A.3: In a simple random sample (SRS) of size n, every sample of the size n has the same chance of being selected.

title: When generalization to a population is appropriate
body: If units are randomly selected from a population, generalize to that entire population; if they are not randomly selected (deliberately chosen or volunteers), generalize only to a population of individuals similar to those in the study.
caution: To justify generalizing, cite random selection of the sample; random assignment supports cause-and-effect conclusions, not generalization.

title: Elements of a well-designed experiment
body: A well-designed experiment includes comparison of treatment groups, random assignment, replication, and direct control of extraneous variation.

items.label: Comparisons
items.meaning: Comparisons of at least two treatment groups, one of which could be a control group

items.label: Random assignment
items.meaning: Random assignment of treatments to experimental units

items.label: Replication
items.meaning: More than one experimental unit is assigned to each treatment

items.label: Direct control
items.meaning: Direct control of potential extraneous sources of variation in the response, keeping their settings the same from unit to unit

title: Bias in sampling
body: Bias in a sampling method is a systematic error in the sampling procedure that results in a statistic being consistently larger or consistently smaller than the parameter it estimates.
ced_evidence: 1.12.A.1: Bias in a sampling method is a systematic error in the sampling procedure

title: Purpose of random assignment
body: Random assignment creates treatment groups as similar as possible with respect to extraneous sources of variation, so each extraneous variable's distribution is approximately the same across treatment groups.
caution: Cite random assignment, not random selection, when explaining why an experiment's treatment groups are comparable.
ced_evidence: 1.13.A.7: The purpose of random assignment is to create treatment groups that are as similar as possible with respect to extraneous sources of variation.

title: Nonrandom sampling introduces potential bias
body: Nonrandom sampling methods, such as convenience or voluntary response samples, introduce potential bias because they do not use random chance to select individuals.
ced_evidence: 1.12.A.6: Nonrandom sampling methods (e.g., samples chosen by convenience or voluntary response) introduce potential bias

title: Scope of conclusions from an experiment
body: Random assignment of treatments allows cause-and-effect conclusions between the explanatory and response variables, but if the units are volunteers rather than randomly selected, the conclusions apply only to the population of units similar to those who participated.
